deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, publ. 1867). It covers the end of the integral section (published Art. 4–5) and the start of the representability section (published Art. 7 onward).

(1) Integral in the narrowest sense. Take a partition a<x_1<...<x_{n-1}<b with lengths δ_i. Assume the Riemann sum S = Σ δ_i f(x_{i-1}+ε_iδ_i) converges as all δ_i→0. Let D_i be the oscillation (sup−inf) of f on the i-th subinterval. Then Σ δ_i D_i must tend to 0 as max δ_i→0. This is the necessary half of Riemann's integrability criterion. Implicit step (mine): S can be made to range over an interval of length ≈ΣδiDi by choosing the tags, so convergence forces this sum to 0.

(2) Improper integrals at a singularity x=0. This continues the previous page, where the orders x, x·log(1/x), etc. were compared for monotone-type f. If f has infinitely many maxima and minima near 0, its 'order of becoming infinite' says nothing about integrability. Given |f| (which alone determines the order), one can choose signs so that ∫_x^a f dx converges as x→0. Example of a function whose order of infinity (with 1/x as unit) is infinite, yet which is integrable up to 0:
f(x) = d/dx[x cos(e^{1/x})] = cos(e^{1/x}) + (1/x) e^{1/x} sin(e^{1/x}).
Verification (mine): d/dx[x cos e^{1/x}] = cos e^{1/x} − x sin(e^{1/x}) e^{1/x} (−1/x²). Hence ∫_x^1 f = cos e − x cos(e^{1/x}) → cos e. Meanwhile |f| grows like e^{1/x}/x along a sequence, faster than any power of 1/x.

(3) §2, change of viewpoint. Earlier work (Fourier, Dirichlet) proved convergence of Fourier series for 'natural' functions, restricting f as needed. The right-hand note recalls Dirichlet's two hypotheses: finitely many maxima and minima, and integrability. Riemann instead asks the converse question: if f is representable by a trigonometric series, what follows about its behaviour?

So f(x) := ½b_0 + Σ(a_n sin nx + b_n cos nx), defined only where the series converges. Convergence at x requires the terms to tend to 0. If a_n, b_n do not tend to 0, convergence is possible only at x where the trigonometric multipliers of the non-vanishing coefficients vanish (strictly: tend to 0). Even so, the convergence set can be dense. Example: if x = pπ/q (commensurable with π), then sin(m!x) = 0 for all m ≥ q. So a series in sin(m!x) whose coefficients stay bounded, or even grow, converges at every such x. Riemann provisionally excludes such series. He assumes the terms tend to 0 for every x, i.e. effectively a_n, b_n → 0.

The right column contains transitional drafts ('wir wenden uns zu unserem Hauptthema...'). It also introduces notation: the series is called Ω and its value f(x).
errors: The coefficient sentence as transcribed ('Wenn die a_n, b_n mit wachsendem n unendlich klein werden, so kann die Reihe nur ... convergiren') is logically inverted. It must read 'nicht ... unendlich klein werden' (a struck/abbreviated negation in the draft or transcription).

'Multipliers ... Null sind' is loose: what is needed is that a_n sin nx + b_n cos nx → 0, i.e. the multipliers tend to 0 along the relevant subsequence, not that they are exactly zero. The m! example happens to give exact zeros.

The claim that suitable signs always make ∫ f dx converge to 0 is stated without proof. It is true provided |f| is integrable on each [x,a], x>0: choose sign blocks so the cumulative integral stays within shrinking bounds.
Passing from 'terms → 0 for every x' to 'coefficients → 0' is not justified here. That implication is the Cantor–Lebesgue theorem (Cantor 1870).

results.what: Necessary condition for integrability: Σ δ_i D_i → 0 as mesh → 0 (oscillation criterion)
Integrable improper function with infinite order of infinity: f = d/dx(x cos e^{1/x}) = cos e^{1/x} + (1/x)e^{1/x} sin e^{1/x}
results.modern_name: Example of a conditionally convergent improper integral with unbounded oscillating integrand
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1854 (same example in the published Habilitationsschrift)

results.what: Oscillating functions: the order of infinity says nothing about integrability; signs can be chosen to force convergence
A trigonometric series with non-vanishing coefficients can converge on a dense set (sin(m!x) at rational multiples of π)
results.modern_name: Precursor of the Cantor–Lebesgue theorem / convergence sets of trigonometric series
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1854 (example in published Art. 7); Cantor 1870 for the theorem that coefficients must → 0

results.what: Reversal of the problem: deduce properties of f from representability by a trigonometric series
results.modern_name: Riemann's theory of trigonometric series (uniqueness/representability programme)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of passages that appear almost verbatim in Riemann's published Habilitationsschrift: the oscillation criterion, the x·cos(e^{1/x}) example, the sign-choice remark, the converse question and the m!x example. The only interest is the draft wording, e.g. 'commensurable with π' and sin(m!x) instead of the published form.

transcription_corrections: 'Wenn die [Grössen] a_n, b_n ... mit wachsendem n unendlich klein werden' must contain a negation ('nicht ... unendlich klein werden') for the sentence to make sense.
'Wir nehmen ferner an dass sie keine Unendlichkeiten [?]' is uncertain in the image. The context, matching the published text, introduces the case where f becomes infinite at isolated points.

'Hat aber die Function fx unendlich viele Maxima und Minima, so lässt sich aber die Ordnung' should read 'so lässt sich über die Ordnung ihres Unendlichwerdens nichts bestimmen', matching the published text.
In the example sentence, '(die Ordnung von 1/x als Einheit genommen)' is a parenthesis inserted after struck text; the reading is correct.
The marginal fraction next to §2 is ½ b_0, consistent with the series ½b_0 + Σ b_n cos nx (+ Σ a_n sin nx).
